after.problem:
The second-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-4y=0
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}={y}^{′}+4y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}={x}_{2}+4{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}.$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
The second-order initial value problem

$$
12{y}^{″}+5{y}^{′}-2y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-2
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{2}(1)=q\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & ={x}_{1}(1)=1 \\ {y}^{′}(1) & ={x}_{2}(1)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-\frac{5}{12}{y}^{′}+\frac{1}{6}y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=1 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(1)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=1,q=-2,f(t)=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q)\cdot f(t) & =(1-(-2))(\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2}) \\  & =3(\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{4}{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
The second-order initial value problem

$$
12{y}^{″}+5{y}^{′}-2y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-2
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{2}(1)=q\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & ={x}_{1}(1)=1 \\ {y}^{′}(1) & ={x}_{2}(1)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-\frac{5}{12}{y}^{′}+\frac{1}{6}y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=1 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(1)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=1,q=-2,f(t)=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q)\cdot f(t) & =(1-(-2))(\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2}) \\  & =3(\frac{1}{6}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{12}{x}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{4}{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
The second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-4{e}^{t}{y}^{′}+5y=0,\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-1
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{2}(0)=q\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & ={x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {y}^{′}(0) & ={x}_{2}(0)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=4{e}^{t}{y}^{′}-5y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=4{e}^{t}{x}_{2}-5{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-5{x}_{1}+4{e}^{t}{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=2,q=-1,f(t)=-5{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q)\cdot f(t) & =(2-(-1))(-5{x}_{1}+4{e}^{t}{x}_{2}) \\  & =3(-5{x}_{1}+4{e}^{t}{x}_{2}) \\  & =-15{x}_{1}+12{e}^{t}{x}_{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

The second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-4{e}^{t}{y}^{′}+5y=0,\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-1

$$

First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & ={x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {y}^{′}(0) & ={x}_{2}(0)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{y}^{″}=4{e}^{t}{y}^{′}-5y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=4{e}^{t}{x}_{2}-5{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-5{x}_{1}+4{e}^{t}{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=-1\end{aligned}

The second-order differential equation ${y}^{″}+3{e}^{2t}{y}^{′}-5y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],\,y(t)={x}_{1}(t),\,{y}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t).
$$

Find the matrix $A.$
after.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-3{e}^{2t}{y}^{′}+5y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-3{e}^{2t}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=5{x}_{1}-3{e}^{2t}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 5 & -3{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 5 & -3{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].$

content.knowledge_point: Writing a Homogeneous ODE as a Matrix Differential Equation
content.problem:
The second-order differential equation ${y}^{″}+3{e}^{2t}{y}^{′}-5y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],\,y(t)={x}_{1}(t),\,{y}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t).
$$

Find the matrix $A.$
content.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-3{e}^{2t}{y}^{′}+5y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-3{e}^{2t}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=5{x}_{1}-3{e}^{2t}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 5 & -3{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 5 & -3{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].$

after.problem:
The third-order differential equation ${y}^{‴}+6t{y}^{″}+8{t}^{2}y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & a \\ 0 & 0 & b \\ -8{t}^{2} & 0 & c\end{aligned}],
$$

and for $y=y(t),$ we have

$$
{\begin{aligned}y={x}_{1}(t) \\ {y}^{′}={x}_{2}(t) \\ {y}^{″}={x}_{3}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
after.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-6t{y}^{″}-8{t}^{2}y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-6t{x}_{3}-8{t}^{2}{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=-8{t}^{2}{x}_{1}-6t{x}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -8{t}^{2} & 0 & -6t\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $a=0,b=1,c=-6t,$ and $a+b+c=1-6t.$
